item.title: How have interest rate expectations changed after this week's events?
item.dc:creator: Giuseppe Dellamotta
investinglive.com
item.description:
Rate hikes by year-end

  • RBNZ: 38 bps (99% probability of rate hike at the next meeting)

2027: 109 bps

  • BoE: 37 bps (97% probability of rate hike at the next meeting)

2027: 114 bps

  • BoC: 31 bps (78% probability of rate hike at the next meeting)

2027: 97 bps

  • RBA: 20 bps (60% probability of rate hike at the next meeting)

2027: 29 bps

  • Fed: 23 bps (92% probability of no change at the next meeting)

2027: 67 bps

  • ECB: 18 bps (92% probability of no change at the next meeting)

2027: 67 bps

  • BoJ: 14 bps (98% probability of no change at the next meeting)

2027: 80 bps

  • SNB: 5 bps (82% probability of no change at the next meeting)

2027: 53 bps

  • Last week's market pricing here. The 2027 pricing indicates the total amount of tigthening expected by the end of 2027, not how much is expected in 2027 alone.

We've got a hawkish repricing in near-term interest rate expectations for the RBA, BoC and the BoE after economic data and central bank speakers. The probabilities for an RBA rate hike at the upcoming meeting increased after RBA's Hauser delivered some hawkish comments that suggested a rate hike could come in November. He said the inflation outlook looks worse than forecast, the quarterly trimmed mean is likely to exceed expectations and capacity pressures are more elevated than assumed. He also added that forecasts are still being finalised and he does not know for sure what the Board will decide, which is why the probabilities stand around 60% and not higher.

For the BoC, the expectations for a rate hike increased after BoC Governor Macklem said the Bank would have to assess whether inflation would return to target on its own or whether it would need to raise interest rates to bring inflation down. That was a more direct tightening signal than the previous message of the Bank just monitoring inflation. Macklem said the risk of persistently high oil spreading beyond energy into the prices of other goods and services making inflation more persistent had increased. For context, underlying inflation has been moving lower in Canada, with the latest Trimmed-Mean CPI Y/Y falling to 1.8%, the lowest since 2020. I think a rate hike would be the wrong move considering the US-Canada trade war and softening labour market. 

For the BoE, the data this week reinforced expectations for a rate hike at the November meeting. Wage growth was stronger than expected, with regular pay rising 3.7% y/y versus 3.6% expected. The unemployment rate edged down to 4.7% versus 5.0% expected, with 102K jobs gained in the three months to August versus 5K expected. September CPI accelerated to 3.5% from 3.1%, above the 3.4% consensus. Core CPI also increased, rising to 2.8% from 2.6%, while services inflation climbed to 3.7% from 3.4%. Finally, the composite PMI rose to 53.1 from 52.0, its highest since February, beating expectations. Business activity, new orders and employment improved, while input-cost inflation accelerated to its highest level since June, reinforcing concerns that energy-driven price pressures could become more persistent amid resilient economic activity.

On the ECB side, we've got some dovish repricing as growth concerns increased amid bond market woes, increasing energy prices and ECB tightening. Today, we got the Flash PMIs for the major Eurozone economies and the data confirmed that economic activity has slowed and the expectations for the coming months have deteriorated. 

Finally, on the Federal Reserve side we've seen some notable dovish repricing as market's focus shifted from inflation fears to growth concerns amid prolonged Middle East crisis, widening credit spreads and persistent inflationary pressures that force the Fed to tighten monetary conditions. The losses in the stock market have also been a major driver of the dovish repricing as an AI-bubble burst would have huge negative wealth effect. We still have the US PMIs today that could change interest rate expectations, so it's going to be an important catalyst. 

This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

item.title: Japan’s 2.4% underlying inflation puts a higher BoJ terminal rate in play
item.dc:creator: Eamonn Sheridan
investinglive.com
item.description:
The debate is shifting from when the BoJ hikes again to where rates peak, which matters most for the front end of the JGB curve. A market that moves from pricing a terminal rate around 1.75% to one closer to or above 2% would be likely to push two-year and five-year yields higher after their recent rally. The yen firmed after the data, but a sustained rally would probably need the BoJ to endorse a higher peak next week, given the large trade deficit and the wide gap with US rates. For equities, a higher-for-longer BoJ path tends to favour banks over exporters. Oil remains the key upstream driver: Middle East-linked energy costs are feeding Japanese inflation even with fuel subsidies in place, so crude above $110 a barrel keeps upside risk on both prices and the BoJ’s forecasts.

---

Earlier:

  • Japan core inflation tops BoJ’s 2% target for first time since December, yen firms

---

Japan’s inflation is now broad enough that a December BoJ hike looks like the starting point rather than the question, with markets turning to how far the bank will ultimately need to go.

Summary:

  • Japan’s core CPI rose 2.1% in September from 1.7%, above the BoJ’s target for the first time in nine months. The measure excluding fresh food and fuel rose 2.4% from 1.9%.
  • Goods inflation rose to 2.8% from 2.6%, and services inflation rose to 1.5% from 1.2%, a sign that firms are passing on higher labour costs.
  • Higher fuel costs from the Middle East conflict, a weak yen and AI-driven demand are offsetting the effect of government fuel subsidies.
  • The BoJ is expected to hold rates at 1.25% next week but may raise its inflation forecasts and say underlying inflation has likely reached 2%.
  • Many analysts expect a hike to 1.50% in December, with a terminal rate around 1.75% to 2%, and some see the risk of a higher peak.
  • The PMI showed hiring slowing to a 14-month low, and the economy minister said conditions are not yet met to declare deflation over.

Japan’s underlying inflation accelerated in September, with price increases broadening across goods and services despite government fuel subsidies. The data strengthen expectations of a Bank of Japan rate hike in December and are shifting attention to how high rates may ultimately go.

Core consumer prices, which exclude fresh food but include fuel, rose 2.1% from a year earlier, matching forecasts and accelerating from 1.7% in August. It was the first reading above the BoJ’s 2% target in nine months, Reuters reported. The index excluding both fresh food and fuel, which the BoJ watches closely as a better measure of demand-driven inflation, rose 2.4% from 1.9%.

The breakdown showed price pressure spreading. Goods inflation rose to 2.8% from 2.6%, while services inflation increased to 1.5% from 1.2%, suggesting firms are starting to pass higher wages on to customers. Rising fuel costs linked to the prolonged Middle East conflict, higher import prices from a weak yen and strong demand linked to artificial intelligence have together blunted the impact of the fuel subsidies.

Services inflation remains the weak link in that picture. At 1.5%, it is still well short of 2%, a reminder that the wage-driven, domestically generated inflation the BoJ has long sought is building only gradually.

The BoJ is widely expected to keep its policy rate at 1.25% at its two-day meeting ending October 30, having raised it to a 31-year high in September. Sources have told Reuters the bank may revise up its inflation forecasts, signal that underlying inflation has likely reached 2%, and stress its focus on anchoring inflation at that level. Governor Kazuo Ueda said last week that the BoJ would not tolerate an inflation overshoot.

One economist told Reuters that rising energy costs and their knock-on effects should push core inflation higher, but that prices are not accelerating sharply enough to justify back-to-back hikes, and he expects the next move in December. Many analysts polled by Reuters expect the BoJ to raise rates to 1.50% in December, with a terminal rate of around 1.75% to 2%. Some see the risks tilting higher. Capital Economics said there is little evidence that tightening so far has slowed the economy and that the policy rate may peak above its 2% forecast. Recent surveys have shown little sign that higher rates are weighing on loan demand.

Not all of Friday’s data supported a more aggressive path. A flash business survey released the same morning showed private sector growth steady but subdued in October, with job creation slowing to a 14-month low and services firms cutting staff for the first time in more than a year. Economy Minister Minoru Kiuchi said conditions have not yet been met for the government to declare an official end to deflation, and he urged the BoJ to guide policy appropriately.

That leaves the BoJ facing a familiar balance at next week’s meeting: inflation that is finally broadening, against signs that the labour market and domestic demand are losing some momentum. How the bank describes that balance in its outlook report is likely to shape market expectations for the policy rate well beyond December. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6758 – Reuters estimate
item.dc:creator: Eamonn Sheridan
investinglive.com
item.description:
The People’s Bank of China is due to set the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time), a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets. China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours. Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day’s closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations. Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility. Intervention can take the form of direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance through state-owned banks. As a result, the daily fixing is often interpreted as a policy signal rather than just a technical reference point. A stronger-than-expected CNY midpoint is typically read as a sign the PBOC is leaning against depreciation pressure, while a weaker fixing for the CNY can indicate tolerance for a softer currency, often in response to dollar strength or domestic economic headwinds.In periods of heightened global volatility, such as shifts in US rate expectations, trade tensions or capital flow pressures, the fixing takes on added significance. For investors, it provides insight into Beijing’s currency priorities, balancing competitiveness, capital stability and financial market confidence. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: ECB preview: MUFG sees October hold, two hikes ahead. See EUR/USD year end at 1.12
item.dc:creator: Eamonn Sheridan
investinglive.com
item.description:
The French-German 10-year spread is the key gauge: MUFG’s scenarios put it at about 170 basis points in its base case and above 200 in a crisis, levels last associated with the euro zone debt crisis. EUR/USD has been tracking the two-year swap spread between the euro and the dollar closely, so any further scaling back of ECB hike expectations is likely to weigh on the currency, while a firm December signal would offer some support. In bonds, heavy redemptions from the ECB’s portfolio in coming months put the pace of quantitative tightening in focus. Any hint of a slowdown could ease pressure on French debt. Energy remains a swing factor: MUFG’s forecasts assume supply risks fade, so persistently high oil and gas prices tied to the Middle East conflict would challenge both its rate path and its call for a gradual euro recovery.

---

Earlier:

  • ECB’s Panetta says rising yields a drag on growth, not a crisis, ahead of rate meeting
  • BoE preview: MUFG expects November rate hike as energy shock pushes UK inflation above 4%

---

MUFG expects the ECB to hold next week as higher bond yields and French fiscal stress tighten conditions for it, but still sees two more hikes, with France the biggest risk to the euro.

Summary:

  • MUFG says the bond sell-off and French fiscal risks have removed the case for an October ECB rate hike, as officials highlight the drag from tighter financial conditions.
  • It still expects a 25 basis point hike in December and another in the first quarter of 2027, taking the policy rate to 3.00%, then a cut back to 2.75% by the third quarter of 2027.
  • Resilient activity and higher gas prices since September justify moving into slightly restrictive territory on a risk-management basis, while underlying inflation remains contained.
  • MUFG’s base case, given 45% probability, is continued French fiscal drift, with the deficit at 5.6% to 6.0% of GDP, the French-German spread near 170 basis points, and EUR/USD in a 1.08 to 1.14 range.
  • In a deeper credibility crisis (15%), it sees the spread above 200 basis points and EUR/USD between 1.02 and 1.10, with the ECB’s TPI potentially in focus.
  • MUFG forecasts EUR/USD at 1.12 by year-end, recovering gradually to 1.18 by the third quarter of 2027.

The European Central Bank is set to keep rates on hold at next week’s policy meeting, but MUFG argues the tightening cycle is not over, even as rising bond yields and French fiscal stress do some of the work for policymakers.

In its October European outlook, MUFG said the bond market sell-off and growing fiscal risks in France have taken an October rate hike off the table. ECB officials have increasingly pointed to the impact of tighter financial conditions on the outlook, and underlying inflation pressures remain contained. Even so, the bank’s strategists argue that resilient economic activity and higher gas prices since September still justify a move into slightly restrictive territory as a risk-management measure. MUFG expects a 25 basis point hike in December and another in the first quarter of 2027, taking the policy rate to 3.00%. It then sees the ECB cutting back to 2.75% by the third quarter of 2027, a path that assumes energy supply risks fade.

France is at the centre of the outlook. MUFG notes that a fragmented parliament has led successive governments to miss fiscal targets repeatedly, leaving the deficit close to 6% of GDP despite several consolidation plans. With public debt around 120% of GDP, the bank says France has little room for further slippage and is highly exposed to weaker growth or a rise in borrowing costs. The IMF’s latest forecasts already show France as the clear outlier among major European economies, with growth seen at just 0.4% this year.

The strain is visible in the bond market. The spread between French and German 10-year yields has widened to levels last seen during the euro zone debt crisis, while France’s annual interest bill has climbed to a record. MUFG suggests that a high and rising share of French debt held by foreign investors may have amplified the sell-off. Contagion has so far been limited, with Italian spreads relatively contained.

The bank sets out four scenarios ahead of France’s presidential election, in which it describes Marine Le Pen as the frontrunner. Its base case, given 45% probability, is continued drift: the government survives by relying on procedural mechanisms, measures are diluted or delayed, and the deficit stays between 5.6% and 6.0% of GDP. In that case, MUFG sees the French-German spread around 170 basis points and EUR/USD in a 1.08 to 1.14 range. It would not force an immediate ECB response, but quantitative tightening could come under review.

A deeper credibility crisis, at 15%, would bring acute political instability, a recession and a deficit well above 6% in 2027. That would push the spread above 200 basis points and drive EUR/USD down to between 1.02 and 1.10, with investors looking to the ECB’s Transmission Protection Instrument as a potential backstop. On the more positive side, limited consolidation (35%) would leave the spread near 110 basis points, while faster consolidation (5%) would narrow it to about 90 basis points and support EUR/USD in a 1.12 to 1.18 range.

For the currency, MUFG says the scaling back of ECB hike expectations has already helped weaken the euro, which has closely tracked short-term rate differentials with the US. The bank expects the dollar to remain stronger for longer. It forecasts EUR/USD at 1.12 at the end of this year before a gradual recovery to 1.14 in the first quarter of 2027, 1.16 in the second and 1.18 in the third.

With policymakers in their quiet period, next week’s statement and press conference will be watched for how much weight the ECB gives to tighter financial conditions and French fiscal risks, and whether it keeps the door open to a December move. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: ECB’s Panetta says rising yields a drag on growth, not a crisis, ahead of rate meeting
item.dc:creator: Eamonn Sheridan
investinglive.com
item.description:
Panetta’s remarks put the focus on sovereign spreads, especially French and Italian debt against German Bunds, as the market’s main stress gauge in the euro zone. If US yields keep rising, the spillover he describes could push periphery spreads wider, a risk for Italian bonds given his own warning. For the euro, a growth gap that favours the US alongside higher US yields is a headwind, even with the ECB still facing inflation near double its target. Oil remains the swing factor: sustained high energy prices keep inflation pressure on the ECB, while the drag from tighter financial conditions points the other way. That tension is likely to shape how markets read next week’s decision.

- With policymakers in their pre-meeting quiet period, Panetta’s warning on bond yields is a reminder that markets may already be doing some of the ECB’s tightening for it.

Summary:

  • Bank of Italy Governor Fabio Panetta said the rise in bond yields will weigh on the euro zone economy but is not critical at this stage.
  • He described the bond sell-off as global and led by the US, where growth and inflation have beaten expectations, while European growth is weaker.
  • Panetta pointed to France’s high debt and deficits as a source of pressure, said Germany’s stronger finances have limited its yield rise, and noted spillovers to Italian borrowing costs.
  • Portugal’s central bank governor Alvaro Santos Pereira called for deeper EU integration in services, transport and energy.
  • The ECB is expected to leave rates unchanged at next week’s meeting, and policymakers are in a quiet period on monetary policy.
  • Euro zone inflation is running at almost double the ECB’s 2% target because of surging energy costs.

European Central Bank Governing Council member Fabio Panetta said the recent rise in bond yields will hold back the euro zone economy, though he does not see it as critical for now. His comments come as policymakers prepare for next week’s monetary policy meeting.

Speaking in Turin on Wednesday, the Bank of Italy governor described the move in debt markets as a global phenomenon, driven over the past week by the US, where both growth and inflation have come in stronger than expected. The difficulty for Europe, he said, is that higher US rates come with firmer growth, while expansion in the euro zone is less robust. He described the result as a drag on growth rather than a crisis, according to Bloomberg.

Panetta also pointed to uneven pressure within the bloc. Germany has seen a smaller rise in yields thanks to its stronger public finances, he said, while France’s persistently high debt and budget deficits have kept attention on the bloc’s second-largest economy. He noted that sovereign debt tensions can push up borrowing costs in Italy, and that higher long-term US rates tend to spill over into European markets, including Italian financing costs.

His comments add to warnings from other ECB officials that tighter financial conditions could slow growth. A slowdown could also help contain inflation, which surging energy costs have pushed to almost double the ECB’s 2% target.

Separately on Thursday, Portugal’s central bank governor Alvaro Santos Pereira, also an ECB policymaker, called for renewed momentum behind European integration, Reuters reported. He said Europe’s difficult geopolitical environment and its technological shortcomings show the need to deepen the single market in services, transport and energy. The single market has removed many barriers, he said, but those that remain are harder to fix because they are rooted in national institutions and rules.

Neither official addressed the rate outlook directly, as ECB policymakers are in a one-week quiet period before the meeting, when they cannot comment on monetary policy. Still, the two speeches point to the same problem from different angles: Panetta to the cyclical drag from higher borrowing costs, and Santos Pereira to the structural weaknesses that limit how much growth the euro zone can generate.

That matters for the policy debate. If market-driven increases in yields are already tightening financial conditions, the case for policymakers to add to that tightening themselves becomes harder to make, at least while growth remains fragile. The ECB is widely expected to keep rates unchanged next week. Markets will watch how much weight the statement and press conference give to financial conditions, French fiscal risks and the energy-driven inflation outlook. That balance is likely to shape expectations for the meetings that follow. 

---

The 2026 penultimate European Central Bank meeting is next week:

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: The market now sees a 22% chance the Fed doesn't hike again this year
item.dc:creator: Adam Button
investinglive.com
item.description:
The Fed funds futures marketr now sees a 22% that the Federal Reserve is done hiking rates for this year.

That's a big swing to where we were after the CPI report, which is the most-revelant number the Fed should be thinking about next week. Instead, the market is focused on how the FOMC will react to the stock market, which is slumping on AI capital raising fears. 

For next week's meeting, the market now sees only a 5% chance of a hike, the lowest this month. For December, it's still at a 78% chance of a hike but no longer a sure thing. January pricing is at 27 basis points, which is barely pricing in a single hike.

Looking further out the curve, the market sees 63.5 bps this year, a far cry from the 80-90 bps priced in earlier this month.

You can also see a major repricing underway in the bond market as 2-year yields are down 18 basis points to 4.64% today. It comes after Meta filed for a new class of shares. The share filingindicates that all three long-term forecasts presented to the Board contemplated raising hundreds of billions of dollars, potentially beginning as early this autumn. Management also viewed an  equity raise as “essential” to anticipated business plans and expects additional near-term capital, including equity.

The fixed income market could be taking a view that AI bonds are now tapped out and capital raising will now fall to equity. That's bad news for share prices and Meta is down 7.5% today but it could also mean less issuance of debt, which could limit crowding out in bonds. The lack of capital could also be causing jitters about the value in the broader AI build out and signal a retrechment in the entire trade.

The problem for the Fed is that a slump in AI capital raises might not be the tonic to curb inflation. The Iran blockade continues and oil prices are up $2.35 to $99.50 today with fuel prices much higher still. That will be plenty of fuel for the hawks and make for a lively debate (and maybe a split vote?) next week.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: Most analysts now expect the next BOJ rate hike in December, none see October move: Bloomberg
item.dc:creator: Eamonn Sheridan
investinglive.com
item.description:
With an October 30 move ruled out by every economist surveyed, the yen’s direction is likely to hinge on the tone of the BOJ’s statement and outlook report. A declaration that underlying inflation has reached 2% would mark a historic shift and strengthen expectations of a December hike. That could support the yen and push Japanese government bond yields higher. Board voting is another swing factor: further dissent from Takaichi-appointed members would likely weigh on the yen, while a call for a hike by a hawkish member would have the opposite effect. Oil prices remain a key influence on Japan’s inflation outlook as a major energy importer. Any escalation in the Middle East that lifts crude would add to the case for steady quarterly hikes, while also pressuring Japan’s trade balance and the yen.

---

Earlier:

  • BOJ seen lifting rates to 1.50% in December as 69% of economists expect a Q4 hike

---

BOJ watchers have moved firmly toward a December hike, and the bigger question this month is whether Japan’s central bank finally declares victory on 2% inflation after 13 years of trying.

Summary:

  • 83% of economists surveyed by Bloomberg expect the Bank of Japan’s next rate hike in December, up from 35% a month ago, when January was the most popular pick
  • None expect a move at the October 30 meeting; the policy rate stands at 1.25%
  • 67% now expect the BOJ to hike every three months, up from 46%, and the median terminal rate forecast is unchanged at 1.75%
  • The key focus in October is whether the BOJ judges that underlying inflation has reached its 2% target, which it has not declared since setting the goal in 2013
  • About two-thirds of economists think Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s government has softened its stance on rate hikes, after the US urged Japan to drop reflationary policies
  • September’s hike drew two dissents from Takaichi-appointed board members, keeping voting patterns in focus

More than 80% of Bank of Japan watchers now expect the central bank’s next interest rate increase to come in December, according to a Bloomberg survey, with none forecasting a move when its next meeting concludes on October 30.

Some 83% of economists expect the BOJ to raise borrowing costs from 1.25% at its meeting ending December 18, up sharply from 35% in last month’s survey, when January was the most popular pick. Two-thirds of respondents also expect the BOJ to hike every three months, up from 46%. That suggests economists see it maintaining its current pace after September’s increase, its second in three months and the fastest tightening since 1990. The median forecast for the peak rate in this cycle held at 1.75%.

Many economists said the main focus of this month’s meeting will be whether the BOJ concludes that underlying inflation has reached its 2% target, something it has not declared since adopting the goal in 2013. Economists at Morgan Stanley MUFG Securities expect the bank to signal that underlying inflation is around 2%, and to deliver a hawkish hold. Economists expect the quarterly outlook report released alongside the decision to leave inflation projections broadly unchanged, apart from a slight upgrade for next fiscal year.

September’s hike took the policy rate into the BOJ’s estimated neutral range of 1.1% to 2.5% for the first time, increasing market interest in how high rates will ultimately go.

Politics remains a factor. Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi is known as a supporter of monetary easing. However, after US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent urged Japan to drop reflationary policies, Takaichi and her ministers said they are not pursuing reflation. About two-thirds of economists in the survey now think the government has softened its stance on BOJ hikes. Strategists at Mitsubishi UFJ Morgan Stanley Securities said the prime minister’s office probably does not welcome further increases, but is likely to tacitly accept them for now, largely because of relations with the US.

Board votes are also under scrutiny. September’s increase drew dissents from Toichiro Asada and Ayano Sato, both Takaichi appointees, which helped weaken the yen. Some economists see a chance that hawkish board member Hajime Takata will push for a back-to-back hike at this month’s meeting. 

Bank of Japan Governor Ueda 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Bank of Korea holds rate at 3% after back-to-back hikes, keeps door open to November move
item.dc:creator: Eamonn Sheridan
investinglive.com
item.description:
With the hold fully priced, attention shifts to Governor Shin’s news conference at 02:10 GMT for guidance on whether November remains live. A clear signal that the pause is temporary would likely support the won and push short-dated Korean government bond yields higher. A softer emphasis on monitoring the impact of past hikes could weigh on the currency. The board’s caution over recent stock market volatility suggests policymakers are wary of adding pressure to equities, which may offer some relief for the KOSPI. Chipmakers remain at the centre of the growth story given record AI-driven exports. Energy prices are a key upside risk to inflation for Korea as a major oil importer. That leaves the outlook sensitive to any escalation in the Middle East that lifts crude.

---

Earlier (preview):

  • Bank of Korea expected to hold rates today after two hikes, tightening cycle seen intact

---The Bank of Korea has stopped to catch its breath rather than end its tightening, with record chip exports and sticky inflation keeping a November hike firmly in view.

Summary:

  • The Bank of Korea held its seven-day repo rate at 3.00%, as forecast by all 34 analysts in a Reuters poll
  • The decision follows quarter-point hikes in July and August, the central bank’s first consecutive increases in more than three years
  • Governor Shin Hyun Song has said policy will remain restrictive until inflation returns to target
  • Headline inflation slowed to 2.9% in September from 3.1% in August, still above the 2% target
  • Exports for January to September topped $800 billion for the first time, driven by global AI spending
  • The median forecast in the Reuters survey sees a hike to 3.25% in November, in line with the central bank’s dot plot

The Bank of Korea left its benchmark interest rate unchanged on Thursday, pausing after back-to-back quarter-point hikes, though strong chip-driven growth and above-target inflation keep further tightening on the table.

The seven-member monetary policy board voted to hold the seven-day repurchase rate at 3.00%, Reuters reported, a decision forecast by all 34 analysts in its survey. The central bank raised rates in July and August, its first consecutive increases in more than three years. Governor Shin Hyun Song said afterward that a gradual pace of tightening was preferred.

Shin reiterated at an International Monetary Fund event on October 13 that policy will stay restrictive until inflation converges with the central bank’s target. Analysts said ahead of the meeting that a pause would slow the pace of tightening and soften its hawkish intensity. They noted the central bank had committed to monitoring the effects of its back-to-back hikes, and that recent market volatility, particularly in equities, made a hawkish decision less likely.

Headline consumer inflation slowed to 2.9% in September from 3.1% in August but remains above the Bank of Korea’s 2% target. Growth is being driven by exports, which are benefiting from global spending on artificial intelligence. Shipments for January to September exceeded $800 billion for the first time on record, underscoring the strength of South Korea’s semiconductor sector.

With growth expected to stay firm and inflation above target, the median forecast in the Reuters survey points to a hike to 3.25% at the Bank of Korea’s November meeting. That would be in line with the central bank’s own dot plot projection, which sets out policymakers’ expected path for rates.

The decision means the pause is likely to be read as a change in pace rather than direction. Markets will look to Shin’s news conference, due at 02:10 GMT, for signals on whether policymakers see a November hike as the most likely next step, and how they weigh firm growth and inflation against recent financial market volatility. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6756 – Reuters estimate
item.dc:creator: Eamonn Sheridan
investinglive.com
item.description:
The People’s Bank of China is due to set the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time), a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets. China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours. Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day’s closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations. Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility. Intervention can take the form of direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance through state-owned banks. As a result, the daily fixing is often interpreted as a policy signal rather than just a technical reference point. A stronger-than-expected CNY midpoint is typically read as a sign the PBOC is leaning against depreciation pressure, while a weaker fixing for the CNY can indicate tolerance for a softer currency, often in response to dollar strength or domestic economic headwinds.In periods of heightened global volatility, such as shifts in US rate expectations, trade tensions or capital flow pressures, the fixing takes on added significance. For investors, it provides insight into Beijing’s currency priorities, balancing competitiveness, capital stability and financial market confidence.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: BoE preview: MUFG expects November rate hike as energy shock pushes UK inflation above 4%
item.dc:creator: Eamonn Sheridan
investinglive.com
item.description:
A hike on November 5 would extend the energy-driven tightening seen across central banks. Any guidance pointing to a February follow-up would likely support sterling, particularly against currencies where central banks are seen as slower to respond. Gilts look the more vulnerable asset: 10-year UK yields already sit at the top of the G7 range, and further tightening alongside reduced fiscal headroom ahead of the Budget could keep pressure on longer-dated debt. For equities, higher rates and energy costs weigh on domestically focused UK stocks, while the FTSE 100’s energy-heavy constituents offer some offset. Oil and gas remain the key swing factor: with household energy bills driving the expected rise in inflation, any further spike in prices linked to the Middle East war would strengthen the case for a longer hiking cycle.

---

Earlier:

  • UK September CPI inflation rises to 3.5%, reinforces BOE November rate hike expectations

---

MUFG says the Bank of England cannot look through this energy shock the way it might like, because the UK economy is simply too strong to make waiting look safe.

Summary:

  • MUFG expects the Bank of England to raise rates by 25 basis points at its next meeting, with another hike in February to a 4.25% peak
  • UK headline inflation is seen rising above 4% in coming months as higher energy prices feed through to household bills
  • Energy prices have stayed elevated for longer than expected and have risen further in recent months, MUFG says
  • A stabilising labour market, healthy growth and elevated underlying inflation leave the Bank of England struggling to look through the shock
  • MUFG says UK Q3 GDP is tracking at about 0.65% quarter on quarter, and it forecasts growth of 1.5% in 2026 and 1.4% in 2027, above IMF projections
  • Higher borrowing costs may have cut fiscal headroom to around £15 billion ahead of the Budget

The Bank of England is likely to raise interest rates at its next meeting, as higher energy prices push UK inflation back above 4%, according to MUFG, which expects a further increase in February.

In its European macro and market outlook, MUFG said it expects a 25 basis point hike at the Bank of England’s next policy decision, due on November 5, followed by another in February, taking Bank Rate to a terminal level of 4.25%. The bank said energy prices have remained elevated for longer than anticipated and have moved higher in recent months. As those costs feed through to household bills, it expects headline inflation to rise above 4%.

MUFG argued that the Bank of England will struggle to look through the energy shock, as it might otherwise, because of the wider economic backdrop. The labour market is stabilising, growth is healthy and underlying inflation remains elevated. Services inflation measures are still running well above the Bank’s 2% target.

The UK economy has been notably resilient. MUFG said recent activity data have consistently surprised to the upside, and the economy does not appear to be repeating the second-half slowdowns of recent years, with third-quarter GDP tracking at about 0.65% quarter on quarter. It forecasts growth of 1.5% in 2026 and 1.4% in 2027, more optimistic than the IMF, despite energy-related headwinds.

That growth is fairly narrow, however, led by professional services and other knowledge-intensive sectors. MUFG said it is too early to draw firm conclusions, but the UK’s comparatively rapid adoption of artificial intelligence could help explain recent productivity gains. The share of UK job postings mentioning AI has risen faster than in the US or major European economies.

The fiscal backdrop is a complicating factor. MUFG estimates that higher borrowing costs may have reduced the government’s headroom against its fiscal rules to around £15 billion. It expects the upcoming Budget to include some offsetting tax measures alongside temporary, targeted support for households facing higher energy bills. MUFG questioned whether reducing fiscal buffers is prudent while growth holds up and geopolitical uncertainty remains high.

The Bank of England’s decision is due at 12:00 GMT (07:00 US Eastern time) on November 5. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Bank of Korea expected to hold rates today after two hikes, tightening cycle seen intact
item.dc:creator: Eamonn Sheridan
investinglive.com
item.description:
A hold is fully expected, so the market reaction is likely to hinge on the tone of the statement and any signal on the timing of the next hike. A hawkish hold that keeps a further increase firmly on the table would likely support the won and push short-dated Korean government bond yields higher. Any hint that the cycle is nearing its end could weigh on the currency. For equities, a pause offers some relief to rate-sensitive sectors. The semiconductor-led export boom underpinning growth keeps chipmakers at the centre of the market’s growth story. A record-scale current account surplus provides an underlying source of support for the won, even as policy expectations drive day-to-day moves.

-The Bank of Korea is expected to catch its breath today rather than call time on tightening, with booming chip exports and stubborn price pressures keeping the next hike in view.

Summary:

  • All six economists surveyed by Yonhap expect the Bank of Korea to leave its benchmark rate unchanged today
  • The Bank of Korea base rate is currently 3.00%
  • The central bank raised rates in July and August, and a third consecutive hike would be rare
  • Economists expect it to keep a tightening stance, pausing to adjust the pace of policy and assess the timing of further increases
  • Strong semiconductor exports are driving growth, while inflation pressures are coming from both supply and demand
  • The tightening cycle may continue in the short term, according to the survey
  • South Korea’s current account surplus for January to August reached about $279 billion, nearly four times the roughly $70 billion a year earlier
  • Announcment due at  GMT / 2100 US Eastern time 

-

The Bank of Korea is expected to leave interest rates unchanged at its policy meeting today, pausing after two consecutive hikes, though economists say its tightening cycle is not yet over.

All six economists surveyed by Yonhap News Agency expect the central bank to hold its benchmark rate, which stands at 3.00% following increases in July and August. Respondents said the Bank of Korea is likely to maintain its tight policy stance. However, they see a pause as more likely than a rare third straight hike, giving policymakers room to adjust the pace of tightening and judge when further increases might be needed.

The economists pointed to a backdrop that still argues for tighter policy. Strong semiconductor exports are driving economic growth, while inflation is facing upward pressure from both supply-side and demand-side factors. Taken together, those conditions suggest the hiking cycle could continue in the near term, according to the survey.

The strength of the export sector is reflected in South Korea’s external accounts. The cumulative current account surplus for January to August reached about $279 billion, nearly four times the roughly $70 billion recorded in the same period last year. The surplus highlights how heavily the economy is benefiting from global demand for memory chips and other semiconductor products, a key source of growth that has given the central bank room to tighten without derailing the expansion.

A hold would mark a shift in tempo rather than direction. Markets are likely to focus closely on the central bank’s statement and on any guidance about the timing of the next move, for signals on whether policymakers see a further hike as likely in the coming months. The balance between growth driven by strong exports and persistent price pressures will be central to that assessment, alongside the outlook for the won and domestic demand. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: New Zealand CPI preview: Q3 inflation seen easing to 3.8% ahead of likely RBNZ hike
item.dc:creator: Eamonn Sheridan
investinglive.com
item.description:
NZD/USD heads into the release around 0.57, having recovered part of its slide to a mid-October low, its weakest level since April 2025. A headline print at or above 3.9%, or firmer core readings, would likely lock in hike pricing and support the kiwi. A result near 3.7% could trim those odds at the margin without derailing them. Beyond today’s number, oil remains the dominant driver: with crude elevated and the currency weaker, imported energy costs are set to keep New Zealand’s inflation outlook, and the RBNZ’s tightening bias, tilted to the upside into year-end.

New Zealand’s Q3 inflation is expected to ease only briefly, with oil and a softer currency already lining up a fourth-quarter rebound that keeps the RBNZ on a hiking path.

Summary:

  • Q3 CPI is due from Statistics NZ at 10:45am Wellington time on Thursday
  • Consensus sees annual inflation at 3.8%, down from 4.1%, against the RBNZ’s 3.9% projection; quarterly CPI is seen at 0.8%, down from 1.5%
  • Forecasts range from 3.7% (Westpac) to 4.0%, with ANZ at 3.8% and BNZ at 3.9%
  • Lower average fuel prices drive the Q3 easing, partly offset by council rates, building costs and food
  • Swaps price around an 80% chance of a 25bp hike to 3.00% on October 28
  • Renewed Middle East hostilities and a weaker NZD point to a Q4 rebound, with some forecasts as high as 4.7%

New Zealand’s third-quarter consumer price index, due from Statistics NZ at 10:45am Wellington time on Thursday, is expected to show annual inflation easing to 3.8% from 4.1% in the June quarter, according to the median of 16 economists surveyed by Bloomberg. That would leave inflation well above the Reserve Bank of New Zealand’s 1% to 3% target band, and only marginally below the central bank’s own 3.9% projection from its September Monetary Policy Statement.

On a quarterly basis, prices are forecast to rise 0.8%. That is a sharp slowdown from 1.5% in the second quarter and matches the RBNZ’s projection exactly. The easing largely reflects lower average fuel costs over the quarter, after the Middle East conflict pushed pump prices sharply higher in the June period. Westpac estimates that cheaper petrol and diesel will take around 0.4 percentage points off quarterly inflation.

Forecasts span a relatively wide range. Westpac sits at the low end at 3.7%. It expects a 0.7% quarterly rise as softer fuel prices are offset by higher council rates, building costs and food prices. ANZ forecasts 3.8% and BNZ 3.9%, while other economists see annual inflation holding at 4.0%. Westpac also expects core inflation measures to remain firm, with some closely watched gauges seen rising to the top of the RBNZ’s target band.

The release is the last major data point before the RBNZ’s October 28 decision. The central bank lifted the Official Cash Rate to 2.75% in September, and swaps markets price around an 80% chance of a further quarter-point increase to 3.00%. ING said it expects a 25 basis point hike barring a major downside surprise. It added that even a small upside surprise would reinforce expectations of a move.

Economists broadly view any third-quarter easing as temporary. Renewed hostilities in the Middle East have pushed New Zealand fuel prices back above their April highs. The New Zealand dollar is also trading roughly 4% below the average level the RBNZ assumed for the fourth quarter. Some local forecasts now see annual inflation accelerating to as high as 4.7% in the December quarter, against the RBNZ’s 3.9% projection. RBNZ chief economist Paul Conway has flagged upside risk to the near-term outlook from oil and the currency.

The core inflation detail may matter as much as the headline. ANZ has said the RBNZ will be watching for signs that higher fuel costs are spreading into broader price pressures. That test will shape not only next week’s decision but also the path into December, when the bank is next scheduled to publish fresh forecasts.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: BOJ policymaker Himino warns of upside inflation risks as Japan nears 2% target
item.dc:creator: Justin Low
investinglive.com
item.description:
• Underlying inflation is quite close to BOJ's 2% target
  • Expect underlying inflation to converge to levels consistent with BOJ's target
  • Medium, long-term inflation expectations continue to heighten
  • Financial conditions remain accommodative
  • Real interest rates remain low
  • Delay in adjusting policy could see inflation risks materialise, hurt the economy
  • Upside risks to prices are high

The remarks from BOJ deputy governor, Ryozo Himino, above are not anything that we haven't heard of from the central bank. It mainly juts reinforces the narrative that Japan is getting closer to achieving its long-sought inflation target and that the central bank now has to be careful about letting things run too hot.

The most striking part of his comments is arguably the warning about delaying policy adjustments. But even then, there's no explicit hint that they are going to push for another rate hike sooner rather than later. And that is well reflected in the market pricing as well.

As things stand, traders are virtually ruling out a move at the October meeting but are pricing in roughly 74% odds of another rate hike in December. That is a rather telling contrast, especially when you consider Himino's warning that delaying policy adjustments could allow inflation risks to materialise and ultimately hurt the economy.

That doesn't mean that policymakers are not serious about their remarks. I would say that in Himino's case, his remarks aren't necessarily a push for an October move. Rather, they reinforce the argument that the BOJ cannot afford to sit on its hands for too long. But that's about it. They are neither an explicit confirmation about a move in December as well.

In any case, the takeaway for the yen is that further BOJ tightening remains firmly on the agenda. October may be a foregone conclusion for markets, but December is a different story.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Japan’s Katayama sees no gap with BOJ, says wage-driven inflation is near
item.dc:creator: Eamonn Sheridan
investinglive.com
item.description:
Katayama’s comments may ease some of the political risk flagged in today’s Reuters poll, where most economists warned that dissent from government-nominated BOJ board members could weigh on the yen. Her description of an economy close to wage-driven inflation is language that supports the case for further tightening, which would tend to support the yen and keep upward pressure on short-dated JGB yields. Her reference to import-driven price rises also keeps oil in focus, with energy costs tied to the Middle East conflict a direct driver of Japan’s inflation. The tension between consumption tax cuts and BOJ tightening remains, and markets may test her “no gap” message against how board members vote at the next hike.

-

Katayama’s message was that fiscal support and monetary tightening can coexist, but the real test of “no gap” will come when the BOJ next votes.

Summary:

  • Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama said Japan is seeing price rises driven by higher import costs
  • She said the economy is on the cusp of a shift to sustained inflation driven by rising wages
  • The planned consumption tax cut and payouts are aimed at cushioning households from rising living costs, she told parliament
  • Asked whether the tax cut could conflict with BOJ rate hikes, she said the government and BOJ are exchanging views and she sees no gap between them
  • The comments come as most economists expect the BOJ to raise rates to 1.50% in December

Japan’s Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama said on Wednesday that the economy is on the cusp of a shift to sustained inflation driven by rising wages, and that she sees no gap between the government’s views and those of the Bank of Japan.

Speaking in parliament, Katayama said Japan is currently experiencing price rises driven largely by higher import costs. She said the economy is close to moving into a period where inflation is sustained by wage growth, a transition the BOJ has long described as a condition for normalising monetary policy.

Katayama said the government’s planned consumption tax cut and household payouts are intended to cushion the impact of rising living costs. Asked by a lawmaker whether the tax cut could work against the central bank’s efforts to tame inflation through rate hikes, she said the government and the BOJ are exchanging views on various fronts and that she sees no gap between their positions.

The question reflects a tension markets have been watching closely. Fiscal measures that support household spending can add to demand at a time when the BOJ is tightening policy, and investors have been alert to signs of political resistance to further rate rises. In September, two board members nominated by Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s government voted against the decision to raise rates to 1.25%, briefly weakening the yen.

A Reuters poll published on Wednesday found most economists expect the BOJ to raise its policy rate to 1.50% in December, keeping up a quarterly pace of increases. Nearly three-quarters said further dissenting votes at the next hike could weigh on the yen, which remains only modestly above its 2026 low.

Katayama’s remarks may help reassure markets that the government is not pushing against tightening, although she did not explicitly endorse further rate rises. Import costs, including energy prices tied to the Middle East conflict, remain a key driver of the inflation she described.

The BOJ’s next policy meeting ends on 30 October, when it will publish fresh growth and inflation forecasts. Attention will then shift to December, where the vote split may prove as important as the decision itself. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.dc:creator: Eamonn Sheridan

item.description:
The fixing mechanism matters most right now because its message has shifted over the past month. For nearly a year, the PBOC has set its daily guidance weaker than market expectations, which traders read as an effort to slow the yuan's appreciation, and in late August that gap reached its widest since February, shortly after the yuan touched a three-and-a-half-year high. Through October, however, the midpoint has strengthened at a faster pace, narrowing its gap with market expectations and suggesting the central bank has eased its resistance to yuan gains. The fixing is still set weaker than models imply, so this looks like a loosening of the brakes rather than their removal. The balance Beijing is weighing is unchanged: a firmer currency supports capital stability and import costs, but too rapid a rise risks eroding export competitiveness while the domestic economy remains soft. The gap between each day's fixing and consensus estimates remains one of the clearest guides to how far the PBOC is willing to let the yuan run.--- The daily fixing is Beijing's quietest but clearest tool for telling markets how fast it wants the yuan to move, and after months of saying slow down, it has lately been saying go, gradually.Summary:
  • The PBOC sets the daily USD/CNY reference rate, or midpoint, at around 0115 GMT, one of the most closely watched signals in Asian FX markets. 
  • China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, allowing the yuan to trade within a band of plus or minus 2% around the daily midpoint during onshore hours. 
  • The midpoint reflects a mix of inputs, including the prior day's close, moves in major currencies, broader international FX conditions and domestic factors such as capital flows and growth momentum, with policymakers retaining discretion over the final number. 
  • If market pressure pushes the yuan toward either edge of the band, the PBOC can intervene through direct buying or selling of yuan, liquidity adjustments, or guidance via state-owned banks. 
  • A stronger-than-expected fixing typically signals the PBOC is leaning against depreciation, while a weaker fixing can indicate tolerance for a softer currency or discomfort with the pace of gains. 
  • For nearly a year the fixing has been set weaker than market estimates, with the gap reaching its widest since February in late August. 
  • In October the midpoint reached its strongest level since February 2023. 
  • The yuan has pushed to its strongest levels since early 2023 onshore and since mid-2022 offshore
The People's Bank of China sets the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT, a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets. It has taken on added significance in recent weeks as policymakers have shifted from restraining the yuan's rise to guiding it higher.China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the yuan is allowed to trade within a band of plus or minus 2% around the central midpoint set each trading day. That midpoint reflects a mix of inputs, including the previous day's closing price, movements in major currencies such as the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic considerations like capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The calculation is not purely mechanical, giving policymakers room to use the fixing to guide market expectations.Once the midpoint is set, onshore USD/CNY trades freely within the allowable range. Should market pressure push the currency toward either edge of that band, the central bank can step in to smooth volatility, whether through direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance channelled through state-owned banks. As a result, the daily fixing is often read as a policy signal rather than a purely technical reference point. A stronger-than-expected midpoint typically suggests the PBOC is leaning against depreciation, while a weaker fixing can signal tolerance for a softer currency, or unease with how quickly the yuan is rising.That second reading has dominated for much of the past year. For nearly a year, the central bank set its daily guidance weaker than market expectations, a pattern traders and analysts interpreted as an attempt to slow the yuan's appreciation. The gap reached its widest since February in late August, shortly after the yuan touched a three-and-a-half-year high against the dollar.September has brought a clear change of tone. The midpoint has strengthened at a faster pace this month, narrowing its gap with market expectations and suggesting the PBOC has eased its resistance to yuan gains. The central bank strengthened the fixing for eight consecutive sessions, the longest streak since 2023, and the midpoint has since reached its strongest level since February 2023. The onshore yuan has traded at its strongest since January 2023, while the offshore rate has reached levels last seen in July 2022. Even so, the fixing is still being set well weaker than market estimates, with one recent midpoint more than 500 pips below a Reuters survey forecast, a reminder that Beijing is allowing appreciation on its own terms rather than stepping aside.The timing has been linked to diplomacy.

The underlying tension is a familiar one. A firmer yuan supports capital stability and eases import costs, but a rapid rise risks undermining export competitiveness at a moment when China's broader economy continues to show signs of softness. For traders and investors, the gap between each day's fixing and consensus estimates remains one of the clearest windows into how Beijing is weighing that trade-off, and whether the recent green light for gains stays in place once the summit has passed.

item.title: More from RBA’s (hawkish) Hauser: Q3 trimmed mean set to run hotter than expected
item.dc:creator: Eamonn Sheridan
investinglive.com
item.description:
Flagging a higher-than-expected trimmed mean a week before the official CPI release is an unusually direct steer, and it shifts the risk balance for 28 October toward an upside surprise. Combined with his view that capacity pressures are tighter than the RBA assumed, the remarks are likely to reinforce hike pricing for 3 November, which would tend to support the Australian dollar and lift short-end Australian yields. His comment on supply shocks matters for the oil channel: it suggests the RBA is less inclined to look through energy-driven price rises while expectations are at risk, making crude a more direct input into Australian rate pricing. Softer labour data gives the doves a counterweight, but Hauser’s framing suggests it is not enough on its own to keep the Board on hold.

---

RBA 2026 dates, next meeting in just a couple of weeks time:

-

Hauser has all but previewed a hot underlying inflation print, and with capacity tighter than assumed and supply shocks no longer something to look through, a softer jobs market looks like a footnote rather than a reprieve.

Summary:

  • Hauser said the quarterly trimmed mean inflation measure looks like it will be higher than the RBA expected
  • He said capacity pressures in the economy are more elevated than anticipated
  • The RBA has to respond to supply shocks to keep inflation expectations anchored, he said
  • Policy cannot target current inflation, but that does not mean current inflation is unimportant
  • September labour data was a little weaker than expected; unemployment remains quite low but the labour market is easing
  • September-quarter CPI is due on 28 October, ahead of the RBA’s 3 November decision

More from Reserve Bank of Australia Deputy Governor Andrew Hauser, who signalled that underlying inflation for the September quarter is likely to come in above the central bank’s expectations, adding to his earlier comments that the inflation outlook looks worse than forecast.

Speaking at Citi’s Australia and New Zealand Investment Conference in Sydney, Hauser said the quarterly trimmed mean appeared set to be higher than the RBA had expected. The trimmed mean strips out the largest price rises and falls each quarter to give a clearer read on underlying inflation, and it is the measure the RBA watches most closely. His remark comes a week before the Australian Bureau of Statistics publishes September-quarter inflation data on 28 October.

Hauser also said capacity pressures in the economy were more elevated than the RBA had anticipated, suggesting demand is still running further ahead of supply than policymakers assumed.

On supply shocks, Hauser said the RBA has to respond to them in order to keep inflation expectations anchored. Central banks often look through supply-driven price rises on the basis that they fade over time, but his comments suggest the RBA sees less room to do so after a long period of high inflation. The RBA has previously pointed to the Middle East conflict and its effect on oil prices as a supply-side pressure.

He added that monetary policy cannot target current inflation, since it works with a lag, but stressed that this does not mean current inflation is irrelevant, as persistent price rises can feed into expectations.

The labour market offered a partial offset. Hauser said September’s employment report was clearly a little weaker than expected and that while unemployment remains quite low, conditions are easing.

The RBA lifted its cash rate to 4.60% on 29 September. The Board meets on 2 and 3 November, with the decision due at 2.30pm Sydney time on 3 November (03:30 GMT, 22:30 ET on 2 November), alongside updated staff forecasts. A trimmed mean result above expectations next week would likely leave a further rate rise firmly on the table.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: BOJ seen lifting rates to 1.50% in December as 69% of economists expect a Q4 hike
item.dc:creator: Eamonn Sheridan
investinglive.com
item.description:
The poll firms up December as the likely window for the BOJ’s next move, which should limit yen sensitivity to the 30 October meeting but raises the stakes around the December decision. The bigger currency risk may be the vote itself: with the yen only modestly above its 2026 low, a repeat of September’s dissent from government-nominated board members could be read as political resistance to tightening and trigger fresh selling. Rising energy and import costs tied to the Middle East war keep oil a direct input into Japan’s inflation outlook, so a further jump in crude would likely harden the case for hikes. For JGBs, the shift toward a 2% or higher terminal rate, combined with fiscal concerns, points to continued pressure on yields.

-

Economists now broadly expect the BOJ to keep raising rates every quarter, with the main risk to the yen coming not from the timing of the next move but from who votes against it.

Summary:

  • 69% of economists (54 of 78) in an October 13 to 19 Reuters poll expect the BOJ to lift its policy rate to 1.50% this quarter, up from 36% in September
  • Of those naming a month, about 80% picked December; only 2% chose the meeting ending 30 October
  • 60% expect the rate to reach 1.75% by end-June 2027; 51% now see a terminal rate of 2.00% or higher, up from 40% in September
  • Nearly three-quarters said further dissent at the next hike could weigh on the yen, which is only about 4% above its 2026 low near 164 per dollar
  • Nearly two-thirds expect the government to keep new bond issuance below 40 trillion yen for fiscal 2027

The Bank of Japan is expected to raise its benchmark interest rate to 1.50% in December, according to a Reuters poll of economists, extending a pattern of quarterly increases after hikes in June and September.

Of 78 economists surveyed between 13 and 19 October, 54, or nearly 70%, expected a move to 1.50% this quarter, almost double the share in the September poll. About 80% of those naming a month chose December, while just 2% expected action at the BOJ’s two-day meeting ending on 30 October.

Higher energy and import costs, made worse by a weak yen and the war in the Middle East, are adding to inflation pressure, the poll found. A period of relative stability in the yen, which faced heavy selling for much of the year and prompted intervention from both Japanese authorities and the US Treasury, also supports the case for a December move. Board member Junko Koeda said last week the BOJ should not become overly cautious about raising rates, now at their highest in 31 years, given significant upside risks to inflation.

Not every economist sees the need for speed. Some argued the economy is not overheating enough to justify back-to-back hikes and that prices remain within the BOJ’s expected range. Sources have told Reuters that many BOJ officials want more data on how earlier increases have affected financial conditions.

Expectations for the peak rate have shifted higher. Sixty per cent of respondents saw the policy rate at 1.75% by the end of June next year, while the share expecting it to reach 2.00% or more rose to 51% from 40% in September.

Politics remains a risk for the yen. In September, two board members nominated by Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, who favour looser fiscal policy, voted against raising rates to 1.25%. Nearly three-quarters of economists said further dissent at the next hike could weigh on the yen, which sits only about 4% above its 2026 low near 164 per dollar.

On fiscal policy, nearly two-thirds of respondents expected the government to keep new bond issuance below 40 trillion yen, about $250 billion, for fiscal 2027, after Takaichi said she aims to hold issuance around that level.

With the Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank also expected to raise rates in December, according to separate Reuters polls, the BOJ’s next decision will be judged as much on the vote split as on the move itself.

A personal note: I write article after article on the Bank of Japan outlook and every shift in economists’ views, but if I had simply written “a quarterly pace of rate rises” and left it at that, I reckon I’d have been 99% correct.

Bank of Japan Governor Ueda
