item.title: RBA’s Hauser says inflation outlook worse than forecast ahead of 3 November decision
item.dc:creator: Eamonn Sheridan
investinglive.com
item.description:
Hauser’s remarks lean hawkish, very IMO, and are likely to keep a further rate rise in play for 3 November, which would tend to support the Australian dollar and push short-dated Australian yields higher if markets add to hike pricing. His acknowledgment of slowing labour and housing data offers the doves something to work with, but his emphasis on inflation expectations suggests the bar for holding is rising. The September-quarter CPI on 28 October now looks decisive: an upside surprise would strengthen the case for a fifth hike this year. Energy prices remain a wildcard, with the RBA having previously cited the Middle East conflict and its effect on oil as a complication layered on top of domestic demand pressures.

---

Hauser stopped short of pre-announcing a hike, but an inflation outlook running worse than forecast and a warning on expectations leave November firmly live.

Earlier:

  • RBA’s Kent says neutral rate is rising, questions if policy is restrictive enough

Summary:

  • RBA Deputy Governor Andrew Hauser said the inflation outlook looks worse than forecast, a bit above expectations
  • He said inflation has been high for a very long time and the RBA cannot allow inflation expectations to move away from target
  • Businesses are reporting cost pressures as their number one problem
  • He acknowledged some slowing in labour market and housing data and said monetary policy is working
  • Staff forecasts are still being finalised and he does not know for sure what the Board will decide
  • The cash rate is 4.60% after a hike on 29 September; the next decision is due on 3 November, with Q3 CPI out on 28 October

Reserve Bank of Australia Deputy Governor Andrew Hauser said the inflation outlook looks worse than the central bank had forecast, in comments that lean hawkish less than two weeks before the RBA’s next policy decision on 3 November.

Speaking at a fireside chat at Citi’s Australia and New Zealand Investment Conference in Sydney on Wednesday morning, Hauser said the outlook for inflation was running a little above expectations. He stressed that inflation had been high for a very long time and that the RBA could not allow inflation expectations to drift away from its target, a signal that policymakers see the risk of price pressures becoming entrenched as a growing concern.

Hauser said businesses were reporting cost pressures as their number one problem. He acknowledged some slowing in labour market and housing data and said monetary policy was working, but added that the inflation outlook had nonetheless deteriorated.

He was careful not to pre-empt the Board. Hauser said staff were still finalising their forecasts and that he did not know for certain what the Board would decide. The November meeting comes with a fresh set of RBA economic projections, which will show how far the inflation outlook has shifted.

The RBA raised its cash rate by 25 basis points to 4.60% on 29 September, a unanimous decision and the fourth increase of 2026. Hauser has been among the RBA’s most consistent voices on inflation this year, previously describing it as the bank’s one big problem and pointing to the Middle East conflict, an artificial intelligence-driven global boom and weak supply capacity as drivers.

The next major test arrives on 28 October with the release of September-quarter inflation data, the last key input before the Board meets on 2 and 3 November. The decision is due at 2.30pm Sydney time on 3 November (03:30 GMT, 22:30 ET on 2 November). With Hauser signalling that the outlook has worsened and that expectations must stay anchored, a stronger-than-expected CPI print would likely strengthen the case for a fifth rate rise this year.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Economic and event calendar in Asia Wednesday, October 21, 2026: ECB Lane speaking
item.dc:creator: Eamonn Sheridan
investinglive.com
item.description:
The data is not expected to be too impactful, but we do hear from Lane later. 

'

ECB’s Lane in Shanghai: three officials set the scene for a 29 October decision

ECB chief economist Philip Lane joins a panel on the international monetary system beyond the dollar in Shanghai today at 04:15 GMT (00:15 ET). It is a closed-door luncheon on a structural theme, so a direct policy steer is unlikely, although the ECB says it will publish the text.

The policy backdrop is well established. The ECB raised its deposit rate by a quarter point in June and again in September, taking it to 2.50%. Markets and most economists expect a hold on 29 October and a hike in December.

Lane’s most recent policy remarks came in a 5 October speech, where he described the recent surge in energy prices as a second wave of the energy supply shock, posing upside risks to inflation but downside risks to growth. He noted September inflation reached 3.8%, with energy inflation at about 19% compared with around 2% for non-energy prices, a split that supports patience on rates.

Bundesbank President Joachim Nagel, among the Governing Council’s more hawkish members, has sounded less urgent than his reputation suggests. He said inflation risks remain tilted to the upside and higher energy prices could keep inflation elevated for longer, but that longer-term expectations remain broadly anchored around 2%. Crucially, he pointed to an absence of inflation feeding through to price and wage setting, which leaves room to wait in October.

President Christine Lagarde has pushed in the same direction. She said rates do not move in lockstep with energy prices, while acknowledging energy is a significant variable. Speaking last week, she said there were no second-round effects yet, but that the ECB cannot wait until they are in full view.

The decision is due at 13:15 GMT (09:15 ET) on 29 October. October is a meeting without new staff projections, which next arrive with the December meeting ending on 17 December. That makes December the more natural window for any further hike, with energy prices and wage data the key inputs in between.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: BOE's Greene keeps banging the hawkish drum, and she’s not alone anymore
item.dc:creator: Adam Button
investinglive.com
item.description:
• Greene: continue to think we should proactively lean against the risk of second-round inflation effects
  • The risk of second-round effects is greater than we previously thought
  • Wage disinflation looks to have stalled at levels above those consistent with 2% inflation

Megan Greene is sticking to her guns and the message is only getting sharper. Her latest: wage disinflation has stalled at levels inconsistent with 2% inflation, the risk of second-round effects is greater than previously thought, and the BoE should continue to proactively lean against them.

That’s three for three on the hawkish checklist, and nothing we haven’t heard from her before — she’s was one of the three September dissenters voting for a hike to 4%, she warned last week that waiting for second-round effects to show up means acting too late, and she flagged 3.5% pay settlements as a problem on October 8. The November meeting is already priced at 96.7% for a 25 bps hike, so Greene isn’t moving the needle on her own anymore but this may also be a clue that 4.00% won't be enough, nor will be the 5.00% priced in for late 2027.

What strikes me lately is that the IMF meetings produced a noticeable hawkish pivot across the board — officials who had been content to let disinflation run its course came out of Thailand sounding considerably less patient. Supply shocks, sticky services inflation, and wage-setting behavior that refuses to normalize are showing up in speeches from multiple central banks. Greene’s framing — that the asymmetry favors acting early because you can always reverse — is the argument winning the room right now.

For sterling, this isn’t a fresh catalyst. The November hike is baked in and Greene is a known quantity but cable is strong today up 71 pips to 1.3373. What worries me is that the Fed hasn't made the same incrementally hawkish shift since the meeting and that it might show up as a surprise on October 28.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: BOJ reportedly may upgrade inflation forecast, hold rates steady at next week's meeting
item.dc:creator: Justin Low
investinglive.com
item.description:
The Reuters report is citing four sources familiar with the BOJ's thinking, in saying that policymakers may slightly upgrade their inflation forecast for the fiscal year 2027 as rising oil prices continue to feed through to consumer prices. However, the central bank is still expected to leave interest rates unchanged at 1.25% on 30 October.

That is not all too surprising after the rate hike back in September. And in fact, traders are also pricing in virtually no chance of another rate hike for next week. As for December though? Well, that is a bit of a different story. Traders are assigning roughly 73% odds of another move in the final month of this year.

And that is what markets should be focusing on, rather than being distracted by the immediate outlook next week.

The report also suggests that policymakers are of the view that underlying price pressures haven't changed materially, with little evidence of a broader wage-price spiral taking hold. In other words, it is to say that the BOJ isn't necessarily all too worried about inflation running away just yet.

As such, policymakers are trying to imply that they do have some breathing room to assess the impact of September's rate hike.

Having said that, the central bank may not have the luxury to keep getting away with this sort of move. Higher oil prices, coupled with the risk of further yen weakness, could keep imported inflation elevated for longer. And if those pressures start feeding into broader price expectations, that will spell trouble for the BOJ if they decide to sit on their hands for too long.

But even so, let's be reminded of the fact that raising interest rates will do little to solve Japan's plight. Another rate hike won't help in creating more barrels of oil to address the supply issue. And with regards to the yen, it's a slippery slope with the effectiveness of intervention efforts already proving to be rather questionable as of late.

For now though, markets are agreeing that the BOJ can afford to wait in October. The bigger question is whether the central bank can still afford to wait in December and also for next year, amid pressures of needing to step up the pace of policy tightening.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Daiwa: BOJ shifts focus from reaching 2% inflation to keeping it there, wages hold the key
item.dc:creator: Eamonn Sheridan
investinglive.com
item.description:
Daiwa’s reading points to a BOJ that is not in a hurry but has not finished hiking, which keeps the yen supported on any sign that wage growth is becoming entrenched. A hold at the 29-30 October meeting, paired with an upgraded inflation assessment, would keep a December hike in play and could lift short-dated Japanese government bond yields. Oil is a key swing factor: Daiwa notes import prices have started rising again on higher crude, and any further jump in oil linked to the Iran war would add to the risk of inflation overshooting, strengthening the case for faster tightening. For Japanese equities, gradual hikes alongside solid capital spending are unlikely to derail the market, though a faster pace would test valuations. Long-dated JGBs, where yields have already risen above 3%, remain sensitive to any shift in the BOJ’s tone.

-

After decades of trying to get inflation up to 2%, the Bank of Japan’s new problem is making sure it stays there, and Daiwa says the answer will be found in next spring’s pay packets.

Summary:

  • Daiwa says the BOJ is shifting from trying to lift underlying inflation to 2% to keeping it stable around that level.
  • Governor Kazuo Ueda said on 16 October that underlying inflation is broadly close to 2% and that a further rise from here cannot be tolerated.
  • The BOJ is expected to hold its 1.25% policy rate on 29-30 October but may upgrade its inflation assessment, with a December hike reportedly not ruled out.
  • Japan’s largest union group, Rengo, is considering seeking pay rises of 5% or more in 2027 for a fourth straight year, with an aim of 6%.
  • Daiwa says the durability and breadth of wage gains, including at smaller firms, will be key to the timing of future hikes.
  • Import prices have started rising again on higher crude oil, adding to inflation risks.

The Bank of Japan is entering a new phase in which its goal is no longer to lift inflation to 2% but to keep it there, according to Daiwa Securities, which says the durability of wage growth will be key to the timing of further rate increases.

At a press conference on 16 October, Governor Kazuo Ueda said underlying inflation was broadly close to 2% and that a further rise from that level could not be tolerated. He indicated that while the central bank had previously been willing to let underlying inflation climb toward its target, keeping it firmly anchored around 2% would now be a central policy objective. Daiwa said the remarks confirm a shift it had previously identified, from a policy of reaching 2% to one of stabilising inflation at that level.

Ueda said the policy board would discuss in depth whether underlying inflation has reached 2% at its meeting on 29 and 30 October. Citing reports, Daiwa said the BOJ is likely to leave its policy rate at 1.25% at that meeting but may upgrade its assessment of underlying inflation to broadly around 2%. That would not be treated as an immediate achievement of the price target, and the central bank is expected to keep raising rates while financial conditions remain accommodative, with a December hike reportedly not ruled out.

Daiwa said there is no need to accelerate the pace of rate increases, given that consumer spending remains weak even as business investment holds up. Core machinery orders rose 5.2% in August, pointing to resilient capital spending, including in AI-related sectors. Equally, it argued that inflation pressures have not clearly faded. Corporate goods prices rose 6.8% from a year earlier in September, easing from 7.6% in August but still elevated, while import prices have begun rising again on the back of higher crude oil prices.

The bank sees next year’s spring wage negotiations as the key test of whether inflation has become established. Rengo, Japan’s largest trade union federation, is reportedly considering calling for pay rises of 5% or more in 2027, the fourth straight year at that level, with a higher target of 6% or more for smaller firms and an aim of around 6% overall. This year’s negotiations delivered rises of about 5%, though gains at smaller companies were lower at around 4.7%.

Daiwa said what matters is not just the headline figure but whether strong pay rises become a lasting norm and spread from large companies to smaller ones. More detail will emerge over the coming months, including Rengo’s basic plan in October and the business lobby Keidanren’s position in November, giving the BOJ a clearer read by its December meeting.

For now, Daiwa expects the October meeting to centre on the BOJ’s assessment of underlying inflation, with evidence of entrenched wage and price gains, and any signs of an overshoot, deciding the timing and pace of future hikes.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.
